newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's parliament approve 1997 state budget.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's parliament approve 1997 state budget.

text.p: The Lebanese parliament approved a 6,433 billion Lebanese pounds ($4.15 billion) state budget for 1997 on Monday with a 36 percent deficit of income against expenditure.

The 128-member parliament voted to approve the budget draft despite a stormy five-day debate in which deputies accused the government of sinking the country in debt and criticised it for repeated budget overruns.
The budget sets 1997 expenditure at 6,433 billion Lebanese pounds ($4.15 billion) against revenue of 4,100 billion -- a shortfall of 36 percent.

Only one deputy, Moslem opposition MP Zahir al-Khatib, out of 106 present during the session voted against the overall budget. Eleven oppostion MPs including three Hizbollah deputies, former prime minister Selim al-Hoss and former speaker Hussein al-Husseini abstained.

Threatened that Hariri might call for a vote of confidence if they insist on demanding a cap on treasury bill issues, deputies approved an article that gave the government a free hand to issue any amount of bills to cover Treasury needs.
"The issue of monetary stability is an essential corner of the government's policy," Hariri said earlier.
"We insist that article six should be approved without amendments otherwise we demand a vote of confidence in the government," he added.
Hariri's government pledged however to inform parliament about any issues that exceed in value the proposed deficit target.
Another controversial article giving the ministry of finance the right to destroy documents and official records was cancelled in an article-by-article vote.

The government has presented the 1997 budget as an attempt to restrain spending and slash the chronic deficits partly caused by heavy spending on Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri multi-billion dollar postwar reconstruction programme.
Hariri said during the morning session that the deficit could be cut and debt repaid by boosting the productive sectors and increasing job opportunities.
About 40 percent of 1997 proposed spending will go to debt servicing and interest" -- some 100 billion pounds up on last year.

Some opposition MPs described the budget as "unproductive" saying the total spending allocated to ministries of industry, agriculture and tourism did not exceed 1.29 percent of the total proposed spending.

Other deputies said the level of public indebtedness was disastrous. Total debt reached $10.348 billion at the end of December 1996, a figure which according to some MPs approaches Lebanon's estimated Gross Domestic Product.
The 1996 deficit overran its 37.6 percent target to reach 51 percent. In 1994 and 1995, the deficit exceeded targets of 43 percent and 44 percent, reaching 57 and 47 percent.
